item.content:encoded:
If they valued such information, then why didn't they at least cut off one of A's fingers at some point? Of, if they were too afraid that he wouldn't come back to them in the future, at least monitor his hair and fingernail clippings? Granted, that couldn't isolate one body-part as the cause, but it would have at least confirmed that all body parts shifted.

Actually, that brings up another question: what are the limits of what he can take with him? I know I'm drifting off the topic of just this interview now, but it raises the question: if he can take a backpack, then he can take the contents of an object he's touching, right? Why not just handcuff him to the storage unit they keep SCP-682 in (with a key so he can hopefully get away from it before 682 breaks out in the next dimension), and the next time he shifts 682 is gone forever. Yeah, it would mean cross-testing, and put 507 in considerable danger, but keep in mind that standing orders are that 682 is to be terminated by any means possible, and there's at least the possibility that 507 could dump him in another universe to be someone else's problem.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Ok, I seem to be alone in really disliking this interview—emphasis on the interview, I love SCP-507. My problem is that the Foundation is supposed to be cold, not cruel. How would you justify cutting up SCP-507-B to the ethics committee? I mean, I know they have little real ethics, but what, exactly, did they expect to learn?

Firstly, with modern technology, I doubt there's much they could find out by quickly slicing up B that they couldn't find out through X-Rays, MRIs, and just plain sticking a camera on a tube inside A. Furthermore, the amount of freedom they give A (rather than murdering him, which we all know is the only alternative) shows that they don't consider him a threat. So, not expecting to gain any information that could be used to stop a rogue SCP-507a hilariously non-threatening scenariothis is, at best, a group of people satisfying their morbid curiosity about whether or not dead parts shift by murdering a teenager.

But, honestly, it isn't even that to me. If they wanted to know that they would have chopped off A's finger ages ago.

So, the whole ending just seems out of tone with the Foundation as we know it.
